newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-WOODS, HUSTON, MONTGOMERIE, STANKOWSKI TIED FOR MASTER LEAD.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-WOODS, HUSTON, MONTGOMERIE, STANKOWSKI TIED FOR MASTER LEAD.

text.p: John Huston bogeyed the ninth hole Friday to set up a four-way tie with Tiger Woods, Colin Montgomerie and Paul Stankowski with nine holes to play in the second round of the Masters.

The crowd at the top were knotted at four-under-par, with Italian Costantino Rocca, who had played 11 holes, and Jeff Sluman, who fired a 67, one shot away. Another stroke back were Spaniard Jose Maria Olazabal, Davis Love and Fred Couples.
Only seven players broke par Thursday in brutal conditions where wind and fiendish pin placements combined to make Augusta National's racetrack fast greens appear fit for Formula One.
Gentler breezes and fairer pin placements greeted the players Friday and the scramble for the top of the overcrowded leaderboard was on.

Huston, who grabbed the first-round lead at five-under 67 with a miraculous 190-yard five iron shot that found the hole at 18, slid back to three under before birdies at seven and eight pushed him past Woods and Montgomerie.
Huston's bogey, however, created the leaderboard logjam.
Woods, the 21-year-old sensation shooting to become the youngest Masters champion ever, began the day at two-under but posted three birdies against one bogey to move up.
Montgomerie, even-par after Thursday, made three birdies on the front side and then birdied the 10th and 11th to reach five-under before slipping with a bogey at the par-3 12th.
Stankowski, who prepared for the lightning-fast greens of Augusta by sweeping out his garage at home and practicing on the concrete floor, started the day at four-under.
He reached five-under before struggling to three successive bogeys. Stankowski then bounced back with consecutive birdies to join the party at the top.
It was clear early on that scoring conditions were much better Friday.
"They're slower now," Ken Green, who was first off the tee alongside Arnold Palmer, said about the greens. "You'll see a lot better scores today."
Green, who shot 74 Friday after an opening 87, added: "Today Augusta is like it usually is. Yesterday was a little bizarre."
One of the early starters bettering par was six-time champion Jack Nicklaus, who posted a two-under 70.
"They softened things up a little," said the 57-year-old Nicklaus, who opened with a 77 Thursday. "Yesterday was hard and fast like concrete. I haven't seen it like that in years."
Two-time Masters champion Tom Watson charged through the back nine in five-under 31, finishing with four consecutive birdies to register a round of 68 and move to one under par for the tournament.
But not everyone was taking advantage of the conditions.

Defending champion and three-time winner Nick Faldo shot a mind-boggling 81 that included a quadruple bogey-nine on the par-5 13th hole, where he made a key birdie last year on his way to overtaking Greg Norman for the championship.
It was Faldo's worst score in 60 major championships. The Briton, who posted a first-round 75, had never before missed a Masters cut but was sure to miss this one with his 156 total.
Asked after the round if he would take questions, Faldo told reporters: "Sorry, no. I'm kind of flabbergasted."
Norman, who was paired with Nicklaus Friday, added a 74 to his opening 77 and looked likely to end his string of 14 consecutive cuts made in the majors -- the longest streak among active players.
"It was just one of those things," said Norman. "It wasn't my week."
Palmer, playing his 43rd consecutive Masters, struggled in with an 87 after a first-round 89 for his worst ever Augusta performance.
"I was amazed that I couldn't get the strength to hit the golf ball," said the 67-year-old Palmer, winner of four Masters, two British Opens and a U.S. Open.
"The people were unbelievable," Palmer said about the fans' response to his comeback from prostate cancer surgery in January. He said the galleries' enthusiastic response gave him mixed feelings.
"It's a combination of it being embarrassing for me not to play better, but it's a great feeling to me to get that kind of support," he said.
